items.title: 61529_Maxine Sullivan oral history interview
items.q: I have an autographed book with Ella's autograph in it... I heard this voice and I knew it was Ella Fitzgerald... I went and sat right in front of the bad.

ctx.x: Okay, also (Inaudible) While you're playing that, we also have more recollections and comments about "Locka Loemand."

Yeah. While I was listening to the vocal, you know, I remembered when I came to New York, Ella Fitzgerald was tops, and she still is as far as I'm concerned. But I think that there was a certain similarity between my style and hers. And, of course, it's nothing to wonder about that because we're all influenced by other singers. And, of course, Ella had been a favorite of mine because even back in Pittsburgh long before I ever thought I'd be coming to New York, I used to listen to Ella's recordings. And I also…

items.title: 61529_Maxine Sullivan oral history interview
items.q: I think a Swing singer, a singer that sings Swing has a tendancy to sing - Ella's a Swing singer...

ctx.x: I think a Swing singer, a singer that sings Swing has a tendancy to sing - Ella's a Swing singer, sing more like on the beat. Of course Ella does a ballat out of tempo and all of that, but I mean when Ella first started out she was definitely a

Swing singer because she had that rhythmic drive there. This is what I like. This is what I call a Swing singer. A lot of singers do not sing according to the rhythm. They improvise, they're not strictly, boom-boom-boom-boom. They improvise around the melody. They also improvise with the rhythm. And that's modern as far as I'm concerned, modern singers.
